title: Nigeria's Investment and Securities Act 2025: Has Nigeria Quietly Gotten Ahead on Tokenized Securities?
content:
“Digital assets” sounds simple. At its core, it describes an item of value in digital form.

Yet in the United States, that simple term has become a complicated regulatory one.

The U.S. SEC may treat a digital asset as a security. The CFTC regulates certain digital assets as commodities. For federal tax purposes, the IRS treats digital assets as property. Together, these differing classifications create regulatory friction.

However, Nigeria takes an interesting approach towards digital assets.

In 2025, Nigeria enacted the [Investments and Securities Act 2025 (ISA 2025)](https://sec.gov.ng/documents/1319/Investments_and_Securities_Act_2025_x9rSXtI.pdf). The Act replaced the older ISA 2007 and modernized Nigeria's capital markets. It also does something the 2007 Act didn't: it recognizes and brings digital assets within its scope.

This is not new territory for Nigeria's securities regulation. In 2020, the Security Exchange Commission [stated that](https://www.sec.gov.ng/for-investors/keep-track-of-circulars/statement-on-digital-assets-and-their-classification-and-treatment/) digital assets fall within its regulatory purview when they qualify as securities.

And that raises a bigger question: Has Nigeria quietly gotten ahead?

In this article, we look at  ISA 2025 and how it treats digital and virtual assets. We also examine what it means for tokenized securities. And whether it gives Nigeria an advantage as traditional capital markets move on-chain.

## What Is the Investment and Securities Act 2025?

The ISA 2025 is Nigeria's new legislative framework governing investments and securities. It repeals the ISA 2007 and establishes the SEC as the regulator of Nigeria's capital market.
Its objectives include capital formation, investor protection, market transparency, and systemic-risk reduction. At its core, the Act focuses on how Nigeria's capital market operates:

- The investments and instruments within its regulatory perimeter
- The institutions that take part in the market
- The powers and responsibilities of the SEC

But why was a new Act necessary?

The ISA 2007 governed a market that looked very different from the one Nigeria has today. Over the years, the country's capital-market ecosystem has expanded. New institutions, products, and technologies have emerged alongside traditional securities.

The 2025 Act is more than a change in legislation. It is an attempt to bring Nigeria's capital-market rulebook closer to today's market. Its significance depends on the role each entity plays in the market.

For investors, the Act shapes the rules governing what they can invest in. It also determines which protections apply to them. For businesses and issuers, it determines what falls within the capital-market regulatory perimeter.

It also sets requirements for raising capital or offering investment products. For market operators and institutions, it creates clearer rules governing their operations.

For VASPs and [digital asset operators](https://www.sereel.com/), the implications are significant. The Act expressly includes virtual assets,  digital assets  in its definition of securities.

## How Does Nigeria's ISA 2025 Regulate Digital and Virtual Assets?

Before ISA 2025, Nigeria's approach to digital and virtual assets was taking shape. The SEC regulated them through its guidance rather than a dedicated statutory framework.

However, [section 357](https://sec.gov.ng/documents/1319/Investments_and_Securities_Act_2025_x9rSXtI.pdf) of the new Act changes that. It includes "virtual and digital assets" in the definition of securities. This shifts them from case-by-case SEC classification to a fixed statutory position.

What does this mean?

1. Digital and virtual assets now have a clearer place in the capital markets framework. The SEC now has a clear legal basis to regulate them under securities laws.
2. The Act authorizes the SEC to regulate VASPs and digital asset operators. The regulation extends beyond digital assets to businesses operating around them.
In practical terms, this means the framework covers more than digital assets. It also covers businesses and market infrastructure.
3. The Act also recognizes digital investment activity built around distributed ledger technology. This may have important implications for tokenized securities, which are central to the tokenization industry. 

This leads to a key question for the tokenization industry. What does ISA 2025 mean for tokenized securities?

## What the ISA 2025 Means for Tokenized Securities

Nigeria's treatment of digital assets as securities gives tokenized securities a clearer foundation.
Tokenization: the process of representing an asset in digital form — uses distributed ledger technology (DLT). If the underlying asset is a security, the resulting token is a tokenized security.

The inclusion of digital assets within the definition of securities extends to recognizing DLT offerings and tokens. This gives tokenization a clearer role within Nigeria's capital markets.
But what does this actually look like in practice?

Suppose an asset manager wants to represent an instrument as a tokenized security. The process involves more than representing the instrument as a token. It involves managing the asset's lifecycle — from structuring the underlying instrument and defining what rights the token represents to issuing, transferring, holding, and settling it. This is where the ISA 2025 becomes relevant.

Tokenization introduces another layer. But it does not change the underlying economic nature of an asset. The ISA 2025 therefore creates a securities framework that can accommodate digital representations of investment products, depending on the characteristics of the asset and offering.

What changes for the company?

The company now has more than technology to consider. It needs to consider other factors:
- Structure of the asset
- How the token represents the underlying instrument
- Investors protection
- Eligible participants
- What regulatory requirements apply

The regulatory requirements, however, depend on several factors. These include the type of asset, the token, the offering, and the company making the offering.

The ISA 2025 does not create a single “tokenization license.” Instead, it recognizes DLT-based offerings, tokens, and products within its investment framework.

The broader implication is significant. Nigeria has created a legal framework that accommodates digital representations of investment products.

This might be one of the key implications of ISA 2025 for the future of tokenization in Nigeria.

## How Does Nigeria Compare Within Africa?

Nigeria's approach to digital assets becomes interesting compared to other African regulatory frameworks.

Across the continent, regulators have taken different approaches to digital and virtual assets. Some frameworks target virtual-asset activities and service providers. Others, however, address digital assets under securities legislation or create separate regulatory regimes.

The key question isn't whether a country regulates digital assets. It is about whether the legal framework can connect digital assets to the securities market and the infrastructure required to issue, hold, trade and settle financial assets.

South Africa, for example, took a financial-product approach. In 2022, its Financial Sector Conduct Authority (FSCA) declared crypto assets a financial product under the Financial Advisory and Intermediary Services Act, bringing providers of financial services relating to crypto assets within its regulatory jurisdiction. Crypto asset service providers now require FSCA authorisation. 

Kenya has taken a more dedicated virtual-asset approach. Its Virtual Asset Service Providers Act 2025 establishes a specific framework for licensing and supervising VASPs, with responsibilities divided between the Capital Markets Authority and Central Bank of Kenya. Importantly for tokenization, Kenya's Act explicitly identifies virtual asset tokenization and token issuance platforms for real-world assets as regulated activities under the capital markets authority. 

This makes Kenya an especially important comparison to Nigeria. Kenya's framework goes beyond regulating exchanges and service providers: it expressly contemplates tokenization of real-world assets and secondary trading of RWA tokens.

Nigeria's distinction lies elsewhere. Rather than creating a standalone virtual-asset statute, the ISA 2025 places virtual and digital assets directly within the statutory securities framework. That creates a different regulatory architecture: digital assets are not merely an emerging asset class requiring a dedicated VASP regime; they are also situated within the country's broader capital-market legislation.


| Jurisdiction | Regulatory approach | Digital/Virtual Asset Classification | Relevance |
|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Nigeria | Securities-market framework under [ISA 2025](https://sec.gov.ng/documents/1319/Investments_and_Securities_Act_2025_x9rSXtI.pdf) | Virtual and digital assets are expressly included in the definition of securities | Creates a direct statutory link between digital assets and the securities framework |
| Kenya | Dedicated virtual-asset framework under [VASP Act 2025](https://www.rba.go.ke/download/public-notice-virtual-asset-service-providers-regulations-2026) | Virtual assets are separately defined and expressly exclude securities and other financial assets | Very relevant because the law explicitly connects virtual-asset regulation with RWA tokenization |
| Ghana | Dedicated virtual-asset framework under [VASP Act 2025](https://www.bog.gov.gh/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/PRESS-RELEASE-PASSAGE-OF-THE-VIRTUAL-ASSET-SERVICE-PROVIDERS-BILL221225-1.pdf) | Virtual assets are regulated through a dedicated VASP framework, alongside the existing securities framework | Relevant because Ghana's framework brings tokenization-related virtual-asset activities into regulatory oversight |
| South Africa | Financial-product approach | Crypto assets are classified as financial products under [FAIS](https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/gcis_document/201409/a37-020.pdf) | Shows a different route: bringing crypto assets into the financial-product perimeter rather than defining them as securities |
| Mauritius | Dedicated virtual-asset/token-offering [framework](https://mauritiusifc.mu/fintech-innovation/virtual-asset-and-initial-asset-token-offering-mauritius) | Virtual assets are regulated under a dedicated virtual-asset framework | Important because Mauritius explicitly regulates token offerings, but through a dedicated virtual-asset/ITO regime rather than Nigeria's securities definition |
| Rwanda | Dedicated [virtual-asset framework](https://www.cma.rw/fileadmin/user_upload/law_regulating_virtual_asset_business.pdf) under Law| Virtual assets are separately defined and expressly exclude securities and capital-market instruments | Highly relevant to RWA tokenization: the law expressly regulates tokenization of real-world assets, while keeping securities and capital-market instruments outside the virtual-asset definition |

## From Legal Recognition to Market Infrastructure

Legal recognition is an important first step, but it does not, by itself, create a functioning tokenized securities market.

A tokenized security still requires the infrastructure to be issued, held, transferred, traded, and settled within a regulated market. That means the question moves beyond whether a digital asset is legally recognised as a security to whether the surrounding market infrastructure can support its full lifecycle.

Interestingly, the [ISA 2025](https://sec.gov.ng/documents/1319/Investments_and_Securities_Act_2025_x9rSXtI.pdf) already provides some of this foundation.

The Act defines a securities exchange or registered exchange as an organised facility for bringing together buyers and sellers of securities, virtual assets, commodities and other financial products, and it also provides for securities settlement systems and securities transfer agents.

This matters for tokenization because the infrastructure surrounding a tokenized asset is just as important as the token itself. A token representing a bond, fund interest, or another financial asset still needs mechanisms for ownership records, transfers, settlement, and market participation.
The significance of  ISA 2025 may not be that it has already solved every infrastructure requirement for tokenized securities.

Rather, it has created a legal foundation on which that infrastructure can be built.
And that distinction is important.

Recognition answers the question: “Can this digital asset exist within the securities framework?”
Infrastructure answers the more important question: “Can this asset actually function as part of a modern capital market?”

## So, Has Nigeria Quietly Gotten Ahead?

The answer depends on what we mean by “ahead.”

Nigeria has done something structurally important.

 By placing virtual and digital assets within the statutory definition of securities, the ISA 2025 creates a direct legal connection between digital assets and the capital market. That is different from simply creating a standalone framework for digital and virtual asset businesses.

This matters because tokenization is ultimately not just a blockchain question. It is a capital market infrastructure question. Nigeria's framework gives digital representations a place within the existing securities architecture rather than treating them as an entirely separate financial universe.

That does not mean the work is finished. Legal recognition is the foundation, not the finished market.

The real test of Nigeria's approach will be whether this foundation translates into regulated products, reliable infrastructure, institutional participation and markets where tokenized securities can be issued, transferred and settled efficiently.

So perhaps the more accurate conclusion is not that Nigeria has definitively “won” the African tokenization race. It is that Nigeria may have quietly positioned its securities framework for a future in which digital assets and traditional capital markets increasingly converge.

title: What the IMF's Tokenization Note Reveals About the Future of Digital Finance
content:
Every emerging technology reaches a point where proving the technical concept is no longer the industry's primary challenge. 

The conversation inevitably shifts from individual innovations to the shared systems, standards, and infrastructure required to support adoption at scale. The internet reached this stage when attention moved beyond static web pages to global protocols and fiber-optic connectivity. Cloud computing followed a similar path, where robust infrastructure and secure service delivery became far more vital than the raw concept of virtualization. Today, asset tokenization is crossing that same threshold.

Over the past decade, financial institutions have moved systematically through the paces of experimentation. Governments have launched wholesale Central Bank Digital Currency (CBDC) pilots; global banks have issued tokenized bonds and commercial paper; and asset managers have introduced tokenized money market funds. Simultaneously, the market for tokenized real-world assets (RWAs) has scaled rapidly. The tokenized U.S. Treasury market alone has grown to billions in assets under management, signaling that distributed ledgers are steadily graduating from proof-of-concept to live production.

The fundamental question is no longer whether financial assets can be digitally represented on a blockchain. Increasingly, the challenge is whether the surrounding market architecture is robust enough to support them at institutional scale.

This critical pivot is reflected in the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) latest analysis. Rather than viewing tokenization as a standalone technical upgrade, the IMF examines the broader financial architecture required to sustain tokenized markets, organizing its assessment around three interconnected layers: infrastructure, assets, and services. Together, they offer a blueprint for where digital finance is headed, and what it means for the institutions building tomorrow’s capital markets.

## Beyond Tokenized Assets: The Three Layers of Institutional Tokenization
One of the most important contributions of the IMF's analysis is that it shifts the conversation from tokenization as a technology to tokenization as financial architecture.

Rather than viewing tokenization as the issuance of digital assets on distributed ledger infrastructure, the IMF presents it as an ecosystem built on three interconnected layers: infrastructure, assets, and services. Together, these layers determine whether tokenized financial markets can operate securely, efficiently, and at institutional scale.

![image](/images/blog/three_layer_framework.png)

The infrastructure layer provides the foundation for tokenized markets through blockchain networks, governance models, interoperability, digital identity, and settlement mechanisms. Built on this foundation is the asset layer, where financial instruments such as tokenized bonds, investment funds, stablecoins, tokenized deposits, and central bank digital currencies are issued and exchanged. The service layer completes the ecosystem by supporting custody, compliance, asset servicing, reporting, and risk management throughout an asset's lifecycle.

This framework highlights an important reality: tokenizing an asset is only one step in building a functional market. Without trusted settlement, interoperable infrastructure, effective governance, and institutional services, tokenized assets remain isolated innovations rather than components of a connected financial system.

For infrastructure providers, this is a significant shift. Competitive advantage is moving beyond token issuance toward building platforms that enable assets, institutions, and financial services to operate together within a compliant and interoperable market infrastructure.

## Infrastructure Is Becoming the Competitive Layer

The market has already demonstrated that tokenization works. The question now is whether tokenized markets can operate as seamlessly as today's financial system.

That shift is evident in the numbers. According to [RWA.xyz](https://app.rwa.xyz/), the on-chain value of tokenized real-world assets has grown beyond $25 billion, while tokenized U.S. Treasuries have surpassed **$7 billion**. At the same time, the stablecoin market has expanded to more than **$250 billion **in circulation, processing trillions of dollars in annual transaction volume and becoming the primary settlement asset across digital markets. These figures suggest that the industry is no longer constrained by the ability to tokenize assets; rather, it is increasingly constrained by the infrastructure required to connect them.

![image](/images/blog/tokenization_numbers.png)

The IMF argues that the next challenge is coordination. Tokenized funds, bonds, deposits, and payment assets are being issued across multiple blockchain networks, each with different governance models, technical standards, identity frameworks, and settlement mechanisms. Without interoperability, institutions risk creating digitally native versions of today's fragmented financial infrastructure rather than a more connected capital market.

This explains why institutional focus has shifted from standalone tokenization platforms to shared, collaborative infrastructure initiatives:
- The Canton Network continues to link permissioned applications across global financial institutions to enable privacy-preserving, atomic transactions.
- Project Guardian, led by the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) alongside global policymakers, continues to test the boundaries of cross-border open-ledger standardization.
- Unified Ledger concepts and wholesale CBDC networks are being actively researched to solve the final-mile settlement problem.

Across the industry, the direction is becoming increasingly clear: infrastructure is evolving into the competitive layer.

For infrastructure providers, this represents a broader evolution in market demand. Institutions are no longer looking solely for platforms that tokenize assets. They increasingly require infrastructure that can support compliant issuance, interoperable settlement, lifecycle management, and integration with existing financial systems. In institutional tokenization, the platform is no longer the product; the market infrastructure it enables is.

## The Asset Layer Is Expanding

The assets coming on-chain today look very different from those that defined the early years of tokenization. Initial experimentation focused largely on demonstrating that traditional financial instruments could be represented on distributed ledger infrastructure. Today, institutions are increasingly deploying tokenization where it can improve capital efficiency, settlement, and operational workflows.

According to recent market data, the tokenized real-world asset (RWA) market reached approximately** $19.3 billion** by the end of the first quarter of 2026, more than tripling from the start of 2025. Tokenized U.S. Treasuries alone account for nearly** $13 billion**, representing roughly **67% **of the on-chain RWA market, while tokenized commodities have grown to** $5.5 billion **as adoption broadens beyond fixed-income assets.

This evolution is reflected across institutional markets. Asset managers such as BlackRock and Franklin Templeton have launched tokenized money market funds, banks are advancing tokenized deposits and deposit tokens for institutional settlement, and governments continue to explore wholesale CBDCs for interbank payments. At the same time, stablecoins have evolved from crypto trading instruments into core settlement assets for digital markets, with global circulation exceeding **$300 billion**.


|  Asset Category  | Primary Use Case |  Key Institutional Drivers | 
|--------|--------| --------|
| Investment Assets | Tokenized bonds, private equity, mutual funds, real estate | Fractionalization, automated distribution, instant settlement 
| Settlement Assets | Stablecoins, tokenized deposits, deposit tokens | 24/7 programmable payments, atomic delivery-versus-payment (DvP)
| System Assets | Wholesale CBDCs | Interbank settlement, cross-border remittance, risk mitigation 

The IMF's framework places all of these instruments in the same asset layer because they share a common objective: representing value in a programmable, digitally native format. However, their long-term viability hinges on their ability to move across layers, settling instantly via the infrastructure layer and being maintained securely by the service layer. 

## The Service Layer Is Where Institutional Adoption Is Won

While technology and assets capture the headlines, the service layer is where the operational reality of institutional finance resides. Issuing a tokenized bond takes minutes; servicing that bond over a 10-year maturity period requires continuous, complex operational support.

Traditional institutional finance relies on an intricate network of trusted intermediaries to handle custody, transfer agency, compliance, dividend distribution, and auditing. Tokenization fundamentally alters how these services are delivered, but it does not remove the need for the services themselves.

The financial stakes here are massive. According to estimates by Boston Consulting Group and Ripple, the market for tokenized real-world assets could reach $18.9 trillion by 2033, while McKinsey estimates that tokenization across financial assets could generate up to $2 trillion in market value by 2030 under an accelerated adoption scenario. Reaching that scale will depend on far more than token issuance. It will require the operational infrastructure that allows institutions to manage assets throughout their lifecycle.

However, capturing this value depends entirely on the robust execution of the service layer:

- Institutional Custody:  Transitioning from simple cryptographic key management to sophisticated co-signing, multi-party computation (MPC), and bankruptcy-remote asset protection.
- Programmed Compliance: Embedding Know Your Customer (KYC), Anti-Money Laundering (AML), and localized regulatory rules directly into the asset's token standard, allowing the asset to self-regulate as it moves between wallets.
- Lifecycle Automation:Automatically processing corporate actions, payments, fund redemptions, and investor reporting directly on-chain.

Ultimately, financial institutions are not evaluating technology vendors solely on their technical ability to mint tokens. They are choosing partners that can automate compliance, streamline investor onboarding, integrate seamlessly with legacy custody systems, and manage risk throughout the entire lifecycle of an asset.

Issuing a tokenized asset is only the beginning. Institutional markets still require the same services that underpin traditional finance. This includes custody, compliance, reporting, corporate actions, risk management, and asset servicing. Tokenization changes how these functions are delivered, but it does not eliminate the need for them.

## What This Means for Institutional Market Participants

Institutional tokenization is entering a different stage of maturity. The conversation is no longer centered on whether assets can be tokenized, but on how tokenized markets can operate as trusted financial systems.

For financial institutions, this changes how tokenization initiatives are evaluated. Issuing a tokenized asset remains important, but it is no longer sufficient. Institutions must also consider how assets move across infrastructures, how transactions settle, how compliance and governance are maintained throughout the asset lifecycle, and how different market participants interact within shared financial ecosystems.

For infrastructure providers, the challenge is equally significant. Success will depend not only on enabling digital issuance, but on supporting the broader operational environment that institutions require. Interoperability, programmable services, regulatory alignment, and resilient market infrastructure are becoming integral parts of the value proposition rather than complementary features.

As the ecosystem matures, value will increasingly be created by platforms that connect infrastructure, assets, and financial services into a coherent operating model. The competitive advantage will belong not simply to organizations that tokenize assets, but to those building the market infrastructure that allows institutional capital to move securely, compliantly, and efficiently across digital financial markets.

## Conclusion: The Architecture of Mature Digital Capital Markets

Institutional tokenization is entering a sober, mature stage of development. The novelty of minting digital tokens has faded, replaced by the rigorous work of building a resilient, integrated, and compliant global financial system.

For financial institutions, this transition requires a strategic shift. When evaluating digital asset initiatives, they must look beyond the immediate tokenized product and evaluate how that product integrates with cross-chain settlement networks, complies with evolving international regulations, and plugs into existing institutional custody and accounting software.

For technology and infrastructure providers, the message is equally clear. The competitive edge belongs to those who build bridges rather than walls. Success will not be defined by proprietary, isolated blockchains, but by open, interoperable architectures that seamlessly connect infrastructure, assets, and services into a unified global capital market.

As the IMF’s landmark analysis suggests, the future of finance is indeed tokenized, but its success will be written in the architecture, not the token.

Further Reading
This article is based on the International Monetary Fund's analytical note regarding the developments, opportunities, and structural challenges within the evolving digital financial ecosystem.

To read the complete publication and explore the IMF's detailed findings, you can access the official report here: [The Rise of Tokenization: Deciphering New Trends in Payments and Asset Tokenization](https://www.imf.org/en/publications/imf-notes/issues/2026/07/01/the-rise-of-tokenization-deciphering-new-trends-in-payments-and-asset-tokenization-577138)

title: Beyond Compliance: Why Institutional Adoption Depends on Market Confidence
content:
Institutional finance has always operated on confidence.

Investors commit capital because they trust the rules governing a market. Custodians safeguard assets because established processes define ownership and responsibility; exchanges facilitate transactions because participants trust settlement, governance, & market integrity, and confidence allows markets to function at scale.

Tokenized capital markets are developing within that same reality.

Over the past few years, much of the industry’s attention has centred on compliance. Regulators have introduced clearer frameworks, and financial institutions have launched regulated tokenized products. Technology providers have built compliance into token standards, identity systems, and digital asset infrastructure. These developments reflect an industry working to reduce uncertainty and build stronger foundations for institutional participation.

But regulatory alignment explains why institutions can enter a market; not why they choose one platform, infrastructure provider, or ecosystem over another. Those decisions also depend on operational resilience, governance, interoperability, settlement, and risk management: the qualities that build confidence in infrastructure over time.

As regulatory expectations become more consistent across jurisdictions, compliance is likely to become a shared baseline rather than a lasting competitive advantage. The next phase of institutional adoption will be shaped less by who satisfies regulators and more by who builds infrastructure institutions trust enough to rely on.

This article traces that progression: why compliance became foundational, what builds confidence beyond it, and how the industry is already shifting toward that broader standard.

## Why Compliance Became the Industry’s First Priority

The early years of tokenization were shaped by technical possibility.

Developers demonstrated that blockchain networks could represent ownership digitally, execute programmable transactions through smart contracts, and support near real-time settlement of tokenized assets. But proving that assets could move differently isn't the same as proving that regulated financial markets could operate confidently on that same infrastructure. For financial institutions, that distinction mattered.

Banks, asset managers, custodians, and securities firms don’t evaluate technology in isolation. They operate within legal obligations, fiduciary responsibilities, and established risk frameworks. Every new market structure is assessed not only for efficiency but for its ability to protect investors, maintain market integrity, and satisfy regulatory expectations.
 
This is why compliance moved to the centre of the tokenization conversation. Regulators have provided greater clarity through frameworks such as the European Union’s Markets in Crypto Assets Regulation (MiCA), while jurisdictions including the United Kingdom have continued to refine their digital asset rules. Alongside this, institutions have launched regulated tokenized funds, compliant stablecoins, and digital asset services built for institutional participation. 

Clear rules create predictable operating environments. Predictability allows institutions to assess risk more consistently, which encourages investment, participation, and long-term planning. Compliance, in that sense, establishes the common foundation that allows institutions to engage with tokenized markets within defined legal and operational boundaries.

Yet foundations rarely determine how far a market can grow.

As regulatory expectations become more consistent, institutions are likely to evaluate a broader set of questions.

- Can the infrastructure integrate with existing financial systems?
- Can assets move across platforms without creating operational friction?
- Can identity, governance, and compliance operate consistently throughout an asset's lifecycle?
- Can market participants trust the platform to support settlement, reporting, and risk management at scale?

These questions reflect a shift in institutional decision making.

Compliance determines whether an institution can participate with confidence in a regulated environment. Market confidence shapes where that institution chooses to participate.
That distinction matters because confidence is cumulative.

It develops through reliable infrastructure, predictable operations, transparent governance, shared standards, and consistent execution over time. Compliance contributes to each of these elements, but it doesn't replace them. Institutional adoption is therefore unlikely to depend on a single capability. It will depend on how effectively the entire operating model supports the expectations of modern capital markets.

## What Creates Market Confidence?
![image](/images/blog/market-confidence.png)

Compliance gives institutions confidence that a market operates within established legal and regulatory boundaries. But it doesn’t answer every question institutions ask before committing capital or building products. 
As tokenized capital markets mature, institutions are likely to evaluate the quality of the entire operating environment rather than compliance alone. That evaluation extends across several interconnected capabilities which includes:
1. Operational resilience: Financial markets don’t earn trust when everything works as expected; they earn it when systems continue to operate under stress. Institutions want confidence that critical infrastructure can maintain availability, recover from failures, and keep processing transactions without disrupting participants. A compliant platform that experiences frequent outages may satisfy regulatory requirements, but it still creates uncertainty for institutions responsible for safeguarding client assets.
2. Interoperability: Capital rarely exists within a single system. Banks interact with custodians, custodians with exchanges, payment providers with settlement networks, and asset managers often operate across multiple jurisdictions and technology providers. If digital assets cannot move efficiently between regulated participants, institutions face higher operational costs, fragmented liquidity, and duplicated processes. Interoperability is less a technical feature than a market efficiency capability.
3. Governance: Institutions don’t only evaluate technology; they evaluate who is accountable when decisions need to be made. Questions around protocol upgrades, administrative controls, and dispute resolution become increasingly important as digital assets represent higher-value financial instruments. Strong governance gives markets room to evolve without creating uncertainty for participants.
4. Custody: Often discussed as a security function, custody is really about confidence: that assets remain protected, ownership records remain accurate, and responsibilities remain clearly defined throughout an asset’s lifecycle. Qualified custodians, transfer agents, and regulated intermediaries remain central to institutional market structure as tokenized securities develop.
5. Settlement: Tokenization can shorten settlement cycles, but speed isn't the primary objective. Institutions need confidence that transactions settle accurately, ownership records remain correct, and settlement integrates with existing financial infrastructure. Settlement is both a technology and a market structure challenge.
6. Lifecycle managemen:. Issuing a tokenized asset is only the beginning. Corporate actions, compliance updates, ownership transfers, reporting, and redemptions all follow — and institutions evaluate whether infrastructure can support these ongoing responsibilities with the same consistency expected in traditional capital markets.
7. Liquidity: Institutions rarely assess assets in isolation from the markets in which they trade. Even well-designed tokenized assets may struggle to gain adoption if secondary markets remain fragmented. Confidence grows when institutions believe they can both enter and exit positions within a functioning market.
8. Shared standards: Financial markets have always relied on common standards that allow different institutions, technologies, and jurisdictions to operate together without renegotiation for every transaction. Emerging standards for identity, compliance, and messaging simplify integration and reduce operational complexity across tokenized markets — they don’t eliminate competition, but they create the common language that lets markets scale.

Each of these capabilities solves a different operational problem on its own. Together, they create market confidence with compliance as one foundation among several that determine whether institutions believe a market can operate reliably over time.

##  How the Industry Is Already Building Toward This

Recent developments across tokenized finance suggest the industry’s priorities are already expanding in this direction. Several signals point the same way:

The International Monetary Fund’s recent note on tokenization treats it as more than a blockchain innovation, extending the discussion to financial stability, market structure, interoperability, and the policy choices shaping how tokenized markets develop.

BlackRock’s BUIDL fund is often cited as evidence that institutional tokenization has arrived, but its significance goes beyond the token itself: the fund operates through a coordinated framework of regulated custody, transfer agency, investor verification, and legal oversight — illustrating that adoption depends on far more than issuing a digital representation of an asset.

Emerging standards such as ERC-7943 show blockchain infrastructure adapting to institutional requirements directly, introducing standardized approaches for compliance-aware tokenized assets rather than treating compliance as an external process bolted on afterward.

Individually, these developments address different challenges. Together, they point to institutional tokenization, becoming an infrastructure discipline — regulation, engineering, market structure, and standards converging into a single operating model built to support trusted digital capital markets.

## What This Means for How Markets Get Built
If market confidence is the defining factor in institutional adoption, it changes what “success” looks like for builders in this space.

Early tokenization was often measured by whether an asset could be tokenized, a smart contract deployed, or a blockchain-based product launched. Those milestones proved technical feasibility, but they were only the beginning. A tokenized fund still requires governance throughout its lifecycle. A tokenized bond still needs reliable settlement and clear ownership records.

Digital infrastructure changes how markets operate. It doesn’t remove the responsibilities that let those markets function. This shows that the next phase of innovation will focus less on individual applications and more on the systems that connect them: infrastructure providers designing for integration with existing financial systems rather than isolation, and standards bodies reducing operational complexity across jurisdictions. Each of these reinforces the others, creating an environment where confidence compounds over time.

The relevant question is shifting from “can this asset be tokenized?” to “can this market operate with the reliability, predictability, and trust expected of modern financial infrastructure?” That shift may prove more significant than tokenization itself.

## Confidence Is the Next Competitive Advantage

Tokenization is entering a different stage of maturity. The industry’s early years focused on proving that financial assets could be represented digitally. Today, the conversation is shifting toward how tokenized markets can operate with the reliability and institutional trust expected of modern capital markets.

Compliance got the industry here. It reduced uncertainty, strengthened regulatory engagement, and created clearer pathways for institutional participation. But as that progress continues, compliance is likely to become an expectation rather than a differentiator. What will set infrastructure apart is the quality of everything built around it: interoperability, governance, settlement, custody, and operational resilience, working together to create confidence at scale.

Markets have always relied on trust that extends beyond regulation alone. Tokenized capital markets are beginning to reflect that same principle.

The next phase of institutional adoption won’t be defined by who tokenizes the most assets. It will be defined by who builds the markets that institutions trust enough to use.

title: uRWA Explained: How ERC-7943 Solves Fragmented Compliance in Tokenization
content:
The promise of Real-World Asset (RWA) tokenization is nothing short of a financial revolution. By bringing trillions of dollars in traditional assets, from private equity and real estate to government debt on-chain, we are on the cusp of creating a 24/7, highly liquid, and globally accessible financial system. But as the infrastructure matures, a glaring, systemic bottleneck has emerged: **Compliance**.

In traditional finance, compliance is a heavy, slow, and highly fragmented process governed by geographic borders and localized legal frameworks. When we move these assets onto the blockchain, we don’t magically leave these regulations behind. Instead, we face a complex web of KYC (Know Your Customer), AML (Anti-Money Laundering), tax laws, and investor qualification rules that vary wildly across jurisdictions.

To date, the industry’s response to this challenge has been piecemeal. Financial institutions involved have developed isolated, proprietary compliance protocols, resulting in a landscape of "compliance islands." A tokenized treasury bill compliant in one ecosystem cannot interact with a lending protocol in another, stripped of composability by a lack of shared interoperability. 

This is where **ERC-7943**, also known as the Unified Real-World Asset (uRWA) standard, comes in.

ERC-7943 represents a fundamental paradigm shift. Rather than viewing compliance as a series of fragmented, off-chain hurdles or restrictive, hardcoded smart contracts, uRWA introduces a standardized, interoperable, and dynamic compliance framework. A  standard designed to make compliance native to the token itself, allowing assets to move seamlessly across decentralized applications (dApps) and global jurisdictions without breaking legal boundaries.

## Compliance Was Never Built In

Ethereum's foundational token standards unlocked a golden era of permissionless innovation. But they were designed solely for digital-native assets. Anyone, anywhere, could transfer assets instantaneously, without needing a middleman. They define how a token moves and how ownership changes hands but nothing close to what regulated assets actually require.They simply weren't built with the structure to address RWA compliance needs. 

This design choice came with a fundamental, structural trade-off: **Blindness to identity and indifference to jurisdiction**.

For utility tokens or meme coins, this permissionless nature is a feature. For real-world assets, which are, by definition, governed by real-world securities laws, tax codes, and sovereign jurisdictions, this design is somewhat insufficient and represents a critical flaw. 

To make tokenized assets compliant, builders first attempted to "retrofit" compliance onto the basic [ERC-20 standard](https://ethereum.org/developers/docs/standards/tokens/erc-20/), typically adding centralized whitelists or blacklists to smart contracts. 

As tokenization matured, more sophisticated standards emerged to solve these exact problems. Standards like [ERC-1400 (security tokens)](https://www.polymath.network/erc-1400) and [ERC-3643 (the T-REX protocol)](https://www.erc3643.org/) made massive strides by moving identity verification on-chain. They introduced concepts like "Claim Issuers" and "Identity Registries" to ensure only verified users could hold certain tokens.

![image](/images/blog/standard-comparison.PNG)

However, even these advanced frameworks suffer from a shared limitation: They were designed as closed loops. 

They excel within their own native ecosystems, but the moment you try to move an ERC-3643 token across different blockchains, layer-2 networks, or foreign dApps, the compliance guardrails begin to fracture. They require heavy, platform-specific integrations, turning what should be a global, liquid asset into a siloed "compliance island."

Real-world compliance isn't static. A tokenized bond isn't just "compliant" or "non-compliant." It exists in a state of constant, dynamic negotiation:

- Can a retail investor in Singapore buy this asset from an accredited investor in the US?
- Does this specific secondary market trade push the total number of holders past a regulatory threshold (like the [SEC's](https://www.sec.gov/) 2,000-holder limit)?
-  How does the token handle automated tax withholding for cross-border dividends?

Ultimately, compliance was never built into the base layer of the blockchain. 

## What uRWA Actually Is

In May 2026, according to a [post by Brickken](https://www.brickken.com/post/erc-7943-final-ethereum-standard-rwa-tokenization), ERC-7943 reached its final status in the [Ethereum improvement proposals (EIP)](https://eips.ethereum.org/) under the stewardship of author Dario Lo Buglio (co-founder of tokenization infrastructure platform Brickken), which means ERC-7943 is a mature, production-ready standard.

What makes this worth paying attention to isn't just that a new standard exists; it's that, for the first time, compliance has a shared interface, not a shared implementation. A shared interface that any wallet, custodian, exchange, or DeFi protocol can build against once and reuse everywhere. 

ERC-7943  defines the interface that lets every implementation of compliance speak the same language. Its development was guided by the public EIP process, bringing together insights from the Ethereum community, builders, and tokenization teams facing real-world operational and compliance challenges.

Concretely, it's a set of interfaces that extend the existing ERC-20, [ERC-721](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721), and [ERC-1155](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-721) standards with a small set of compliance-specific functions. It doesn't replace those standards or require migrating away from them. A uRWA-compliant token is still fundamentally an ERC-20 or ERC-721 token, just with additional functions layered on top.

The design rests on three principles that show up throughout the spec:
- Minimalism: Only the functions that nearly every regulated asset needs are standardized. Everything else (the actual KYC provider, the jurisdiction rules, the sanctions screening logic) stays out of scope entirely.
- Neutrality: The standard doesn't mandate a specific identity provider, compliance vendor, or jurisdictional framework. It simply defines how to ask a token whether an action is permitted, not how that answer gets computed.
- Composability: Because it builds on top of existing token standards rather than replacing them, it integrates with infrastructure that already exists instead of requiring the ecosystem to start over.

The clearest way to think about it: uRWA isn't a universal compliance engine. It's a universal plug. What's on the other end of that plug (which KYC provides, which jurisdiction's rules, which sanctions list) is entirely up to the issuer. The standard just guarantees that whatever they choose, it answers questions the same way every other uRWA token does.

In ERC-7943, compliance moves away from proprietary, vendor-controlled "closed gardens." By serving as a neutral and standardized abstraction layer, it breaks down the "compliance islands" and opens the door for cross-protocol, cross-jurisdiction utility without exposing issuers to regulatory risk.

## Inside the Standard: The Functions That Make Compliance Work

To understand how ERC-7943 operates, we must look at both its systemic architecture and its technical API.

ERC-7943 achieves its versatility by separating concerns into three highly distinct layers:

![image](/images/blog/Integrators.png)

1. The Integrators (wallets, exchanges, DeFi apps): These actors don't need to know how compliance logic is evaluated. They simply query the standard token to find out if an action is permitted and if any restrictions apply.
2. The Token (ERC-7943 Layer): Sits directly on top of the ERC-20/721/1155 protocol. It exposes standard compliance methods and emits predictable events.
3. The Policy & Identity Layer (Agnostic): This is where individual issuers embed their localized rules, jurisdiction restrictions, whitelist mappings, and KYC credentials. The token interacts with this logic dynamically when a transaction is initialized.

At the heart of the standard are a handful of highly optimized, minimal interface hooks that manage real-world rules:

1. `canSend` and `canReceive` are account-level eligibility checks. They ask a simple question — is this wallet allowed to send or receive tokens at all independent of any specific transaction?. This is typically where KYC, KYB, and AML checks live. Critically, the two are kept separate rather than collapsed into one check, which matters more than it might first appear: it allows for one-way restrictions that are common in regulated environments. An account whose KYC has expired might still be allowed to send tokens it already holds, while being blocked from receiving new ones until it re-verifies.

2. `canTransfer` operates at a different level. Rather than asking whether an account is generally eligible, it asks whether this specific transfer — this sender, this recipient, this amount — is permitted right now. It accounts for frozen balances, transfer limits, and counterparty restrictions all at once. Notably, the standard requires `canTransfer` to also run the `canSend` and `canReceive` checks internally, closing a gap left open by some earlier compliance standards that didn't enforce this consistently.

3. `getFrozenTokens` and `setFrozenTokens` handle temporary locks. A regulator investigating an account, a court proceeding, or an internal compliance hold can freeze part — or all — of a balance without seizing it outright. `getFrozenTokens` reports how much is currently locked; `setFrozenTokens` applies or lifts that lock. Both functions are restricted to authorized roles, so no holder can freeze or unfreeze their own balance.

4. `forcedTransfer` is the standard's enforcement mechanism. It allows an authorized party to move tokens out of a wallet without that wallet's consent — the on-chain equivalent of a court-ordered seizure or an emergency recovery action. Like the freezing functions, access is tightly restricted, and every forced transfer emits an event, leaving a permanent, auditable record of when and why it happened.

Together, these six functions do something Ethereum's base standards never could: they give compliance a shared vocabulary. A wallet built to recognize `canSend` and `canReceive` doesn't need a separate integration for every issuer's token — it asks the same questions and gets answers in the same shape, regardless of which compliance stack sits behind the contract.

## Why This Matters for Institutions and Builders

The completion and finalization of ERC-7943 is a catalyst for institutional tokenization. Its impact directly changes the business model of security token offerings across several major fronts:
1. Eliminating Vendor Lock-in: previously, if an institution tokenized real estate via Vendor A, they were married to Vendor A's internal, proprietary identity registry and compliance contracts. Migrating away would require a costly, legally exhaustive token redeployment. Under ERC-7943, institutions can completely switch out their identity verification vendor or compliance engines in the background without affecting the token's outer integration paths.

2. Radical Reduction in Integration Costs: for major market infrastructure players like Coinbase Custody, Fireblocks, or decentralized yield protocols, writing custom integration code for every single issuer's proprietary compliance framework was an economic and technical impossibility.
  By consolidating on a single standard wrapper, third-party infrastructure teams only need to implement ERC-7943 standard checks once. Any compliant token built using this standard instantly inherits native custody, transfer, and exchange capabilities across the entire global ecosystem.

3. Preserving DeFi Composability: perhaps the most crucial breakthrough is that ERC-7943 bridges the gap between raw compliance and DeFi's "money legos." Because it wraps around ERC-20, ERC-721, and ERC-1155, these assets don’t lose their permissioned integrity when exposed to DeFi. An investor can pool an ERC-7943 token into an AMM or put it up as collateral in a lending protocol, provided both the protocol routing mechanics and the active wallet addresses satisfy the underlying verification checks.

4.  Compliance and legal teams get something concrete to point to: the standard's events — `Frozen`, `ForcedTransfer` — create a consistent, auditable trail of enforcement actions. That's a meaningfully different conversation with regulators and auditors than explaining a bespoke, platform-specific permission system from scratch. 

## Conclusion
Real-World Asset tokenization is moving away from the era of experimental sandbox pilots and entering the phase of systemic global infrastructure. To support trillions of dollars in liquidity, we must acknowledge that compliance and code must operate hand-in-hand.
uRWA doesn't finish the job of compliant tokenization. Issuers still have to bring their own KYC providers, sanctions screening, and jurisdictional logic. What it does is remove the need to reinvent the plumbing every time a new platform enters the market.

By building compliance natively into the token interface, ERC-7943 (uRWA) provides a standardized language for wallets, institutions, regulators, and developers to align upon.

title: Canton Network: The Privacy-First Blockchain for Institutional Finance
content:
When the history of digital finance is written, the early decades of the twenty-first century will be remembered for a strange paradox: its transparency. Every major breakthrough of the first blockchain wave, from the birth of Bitcoin to the rise of Ethereum, was celebrated for its radical, uncompromising transparency. 

The ability for anyone, anywhere, to audit the entire ledger was hailed as the ultimate antidote to the closed-door opacity of traditional finance. The same transparency that makes blockchains trustworthy makes them unusable for some financial institutions managing trillions of dollars. This transparency represents a structural barrier, not a feature.

The Canton Network was designed specifically to resolve this tension, pioneering a model where privacy is built directly into the ledger's core architecture rather than treated as an afterthought. 

**The Transparency Paradox** 

![image](/images/blog/blockchain_institution.jpg)

For a multinational bank or an asset manager, broadcasting transaction details to a public blockchain network is more than a competitive vulnerability, it’s a compliance violation. A fund manager cannot allow rivals to front-run their trade sizes or timing; a commercial bank cannot legally expose its clients' historical transactions on a public chain; and a clearing house cannot risk the legal ambiguity of decentralized public consensus. 

To bridge the gap between digital assets and institutional finance, the industry needed a new class of infrastructure: a network where privacy is not an add-on or an encryption wrapper, but the foundational architecture.

## When “Transparency” is a compliance violation
To understand why institutions can't use public blockchains for their core operations, one must look at the strict regulatory and commercial frameworks that govern global capital markets. Financial institutions operate under a complex web of fiduciary duties, confidentiality agreements, and strict legal mandates. In this environment, the open-ledger model of traditional public blockchains is fundamentally incompatible with institutional operations.

![image](/images/blog/public_vs_canton.jpg)

1. The Conflict with Privacy Regulations and Data Minimization: Under frameworks like the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and similar sovereign mandates worldwide, financial enterprises are legally required to practice[ data minimization](https://www.kiteworks.com/risk-compliance-glossary/data-minimization/). They must ensure that personal and transaction data is only stored where necessary and can be erased when required (the "right to be forgotten"). 

    On a public, immutable ledger, data cannot be deleted. Even if wallet addresses are pseudonymous, advanced chain-analysis tools can easily deanonymize corporate actors and high-net-worth clients, resulting in catastrophic breaches of confidentiality and severe regulatory penalties.

2. The Risk of Front-Running and Information Leakage: In capital markets, information is the ultimate commodity. If an investment bank begins accumulating a massive position in a specific asset class, exposing that movement on-chain even in real-time pseudonymity allows high-frequency traders and competitors to decipher the strategy.

    They can front-run the order book, driving up asset prices before the bank can complete its accumulation. The public nature of smart contract execution means that competitive intelligence is constantly leaked to the wider market, destroying the alpha that asset managers spend millions of dollars to generate.

3. The Counterparty Exposure Problem: Knowing who a financial institution transacts with is proprietary commercial intelligence. On public blockchains, the graph of transactions between addresses reveals the exact network of counterparties, liquidity providers, and credit relationships an institution maintains.

    Exposing these bilateral relationships on a public ledger compromises proprietary business networks and gives competitors an unfair advantage in negotiating terms and sourcing liquidity.

4.  The Audit Paradox: Shared vs. Public Verification: Institutions do not reject auditability; they actively require it. However, they need selective auditability: the ability to prove compliance, asset backing, and transaction validity to authorized regulators, tax authorities, and internal auditors, without broadcasting that same proof to the general public. 

    Public blockchains conflate validation with exposure: to prove a transaction is valid to the network, the details must be verified by a decentralized set of validators, thereby exposing the contract state to third parties.

## What Canton Network Actually Is

The Canton Network is the culmination of over a decade of rigorous research and development in smart contract languages and distributed ledger technology. Rather than trying to force public consensus mechanisms to fit institutional needs, or building siloed, non-interoperable private blockchains, Canton represents an entirely new category: a "network of networks" that bridges the gap between privacy and openness.

At its core, Canton is a permissionless network of permissioned subnets. This means that any institution, consortium, or technology provider can build and operate their own private application (a subnet) with its own rules, validators, and regulatory compliance frameworks. Crucially, these subnets are not isolated islands. They are linked by the Canton Global Synchronizer—a decentralized coordination layer that facilitates atomic transactions across subnets without exposing the underlying data to the synchronizer itself.

When Canton launched, the participants involved were not speculative startups or retail-focused protocols. The network was backed by a powerhouse consortium of global financial infrastructure giants, including Goldman Sachs, BNP Paribas, Broadridge, Cboe Global Markets, Deutsche Börse Group, S&P Global, Microsoft, Moody's, and Euroclear. These institutions recognized that Canton solved the fundamental architectural trade-off that had plagued enterprise blockchain adoption for years.

To understand Canton's breakthrough, one must grasp a key architectural distinction: **Canton is not a private blockchain. It is a public network with private execution.**

On a traditional private blockchain (like Hyperledger Fabric or R3 Corda), privacy is achieved by restricting access to the network itself, creating isolated silos that struggle to interoperate safely with the wider world. 

Canton, however, allows anyone to join the global network, but keeps the execution of smart contracts completely private to the participating counterparties. It delivers the open connectivity of a public network alongside the strict, ironclad privacy of a local database.

## Canton’s Daml & The Sub-Ledger Model

The magic of the Canton Network lies in its unique technical stack, which combines the [Daml](https://docs.digitalasset.com/) smart contract language with a revolutionary sub-transaction privacy model and localized sub-ledger architecture. Together, these technologies ensure that financial data is shared strictly on a "need-to-know" basis.

A. Code-Level Privacy: Unlike Ethereum’s Solidity, which executes code globally across all nodes and relies on complex access-control layers added on top of the contract, Daml is designed from the ground up for multi-party agreements.

Daml is an open-source functional smart contract language that encodes read and write permissions directly into the contract’s data model. When you write a smart contract in Daml, you must explicitly define:
1. Signatories: The parties whose consent is required to create or modify the contract.
2. Observers: The parties who have the right to view the contract’s state.
3. Controllers: The parties who have the right to execute specific choices (actions) within the contract.

Because privacy is defined at the language level, it is mathematically impossible for a party to view, modify, or interact with a contract unless they have been explicitly granted permission within the contract code itself.

B. Sub-Transaction Privacy and the Blind Synchronizer: In traditional blockchains, even if payload data is encrypted, metadata such as transaction timing, sender and receiver addresses, and the size of the transaction is broadcast to the network to prevent double-spending. This metadata is highly vulnerable to traffic analysis.

Canton solves this through sub-transaction privacy. When a complex multi-party transaction occurs, Canton splits the transaction into smaller, cryptographic components called "sub-transactions." Each participant only receives and signs the specific sub-transactions that apply to them.

The Canton Global Synchronizer acts as a "blind coordinator." It sequences and routes these encrypted sub-transactions to guarantee they occur in the correct order, preventing double-spending without ever knowing who the counterparties are, what assets are being moved, or what the contract contains. The synchronizer only verifies cryptographic proofs of validity, leaving the actual transaction data strictly in the hands of the counterparties.

C. The Sub-Ledger Model: Rather than maintaining a single, shared global ledger state that every node must store, Canton uses a sub-ledger model. Each participant runs their own Canton validator node, which maintains a private, localized database representing their "view" of the global virtual ledger.

Your validator node only stores the contracts and transactions in which you are a signatory, observer, or controller. If you are not a party to a transaction, your validator has absolutely no record of its existence. This means that the global ledger is not a single database, but a decentralized web of interlocking, private sub-ledgers that are cryptographically synchronized on demand.

D. Data Minimization and GDPR Compliance: This architectural framework makes Canton uniquely compatible with GDPR and other strict data privacy laws. Because data is stored locally on the validators of the participating counterparties—rather than distributed across hundreds of random nodes worldwide—institutions can easily comply with data localization laws, execute data deletion requests, and enforce strict access control. Canton ensures that the principle of data minimization is maintained at every step of the digital asset lifecycle.

*"Codify read permissions at every step of a transaction with Daml smart contracts. Canton synchronizes contract execution on a strict need-to-know basis so parties only ever see what they are entitled to see." — Digital Asset.*

Canton’s Institutional Validation Actually Means
In the world of financial infrastructure, there is no greater validator than the [Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC)](https://www.dtcc.com/). As the premier post-trade market infrastructure for the global financial services industry, the DTCC processes the vast majority of securities transactions in the United States, settling trillions of dollars in trade volume every day. It is, quite literally, the plumbing of global capital markets.

For years, skeptics argued that enterprise blockchain projects were perpetual pilots—destined to remain in sandbox testing environments without ever touching real, systemic financial flows. That narrative changed permanently in December 2025, when the DTCC announced a ground-breaking partnership with Digital Asset to build and launch an institutional platform to tokenize DTC-custodied US Treasury securities natively on the Canton Network.

## Why DTCC Chose Canton Over Other Alternatives

- Uncompromising Data Confidentiality: US Treasuries represent the bedrock of global collateral. Bilateral repo markets require total privacy regarding transaction sizes and counterparties to prevent market manipulation. Canton’s sub-transaction privacy ensures these details remain confidential.
- True Legal Finality via ComposerX: Unlike public chains that rely on probabilistic finality (where a transaction is only "final" after a certain number of blocks are mined), Canton offers immediate, deterministic, and legally binding settlement finality.
- Demonstrated 24/7/365 Settlement: In August 2025, Canton proved its capacity to handle intraday and weekend liquidity demands, executing live, automated treasury repo transactions on a Saturday—a feat impossible under traditional bank-rail constraints.
- Unmatched Security Due Diligence: The DTCC’s mandate is systemic risk reduction. Its adoption of Canton represents years of deep technical auditing, proving that the network’s security, scaling, and recovery capabilities meet the highest standards of systemic financial infrastructure.

As noted in[ research by TRM Labs](https://www.trmlabs.com/resources/blog/dtcc-canton-and-the-next-phase-of-tokenized-market-infrastructure), when systemic institutions of this caliber select a technology stack, it functions as a powerful industry signal. It provides the ultimate validation for the underlying architecture, indicating to the rest of the global financial market that the technical, legal, and operational questions surrounding blockchain technology have been successfully resolved.

## A Powerful Ecosystem of Global Builders
Canton’s institutional momentum is not limited to the DTCC. A vast ecosystem of global financial giants is actively building and processing live volume on Canton rails.

![image](/images/blog/adoption_landscape.jpg)

## Where Non-Privacy Blockchains Can't Go: The Canton Use Case

There is a massive class of financial instruments and transaction structures that will simply never exist on a public, transparent blockchain. These use cases require absolute, non-negotiable privacy alongside seamless, multi-subnet interoperability—making Canton genuinely viable architecture.

1. Sovereign Wealth Fund Portfolios: Sovereign wealth funds manage hundreds of billions of dollars on behalf of nations. When these funds rebalance their portfolios, shift allocations, or acquire large equity stakes, they must mask their movements to prevent market disruption and predatory trading. Canton allows these funds to tokenize their portfolios and execute trades privately, enjoying the benefits of instant on-chain settlement without tipping off the global market.

2. Cross-Border Collateral Mobility: In times of market stress, institutions must move high-quality collateral (such as sovereign debt) across borders to satisfy margin calls and secure liquidity. Doing so requires bilateral agreements where the exact terms, haircut rates, and asset identities remain strictly confidential. Canton enables cross-border, cross-subnet collateral mobility, allowing assets to move atomically from a European custodian to a US broker-dealer without revealing the commercial relationship to the public.

3. Intraday and After-Hours Repo Markets: Traditional repo markets close when the banking system shuts down for the weekend. Yet, financial risks do not sleep. Canton's successful live execution of weekend treasury repo transactions in August 2025 proved that institutions can access private, intraday, and after-hours liquidity. This allows treasury desks to manage risk 24/7 without exposing their temporary liquidity needs to competitors.

4. Tokenized Bonds for Family Offices and HNWIs: High-net-worth individuals (HNWIs) and family offices are subject to strict wealth preservation and fiduciary privacy guidelines. When investing in tokenized private credit or boutique bond issuances, these entities demand that their asset holdings and personal identities remain completely shielded from public view. Canton provides the digital rails to issue these exclusive assets while respecting the absolute confidentiality required by elite wealth managers.

5.  Bilateral Over-the-Counter (OTC) Derivatives: Bilateral OTC derivatives,such as custom interest rate swaps or credit default swaps are negotiated privately between two counterparties. The custom terms, strike prices, and collateralization schedules are highly sensitive proprietary data. Canton allows counterparties to model, execute, and settle these complex derivative contracts natively on-chain, keeping the contract state visible only to the two parties and their respective regulators.

## Why Sereel Builds on Canton and What That Means for You

At Sereel, our mission has always been clear: to build the most secure, reliable, and accessible infrastructure for tokenized real-world assets that adapt to the need of various institutions. This year, [Sereel became a validator on Canton](https://www.sereel.com/blog/15).

While public blockchains have accelerated innovation by offering transparency, interoperability, and broad market access, not every institution wants every transaction or asset detail exposed to the public. Financial institutions, asset managers, and enterprises often operate under strict regulatory, privacy, and confidentiality requirements that demand a different approach.

This is where Canton Network comes in. As a privacy-enabled blockchain designed for regulated financial markets, Canton allows institutions to tokenize and manage assets while maintaining control over sensitive information. Participants can transact with confidence, knowing that transaction data is only shared with relevant parties rather than the entire network. 

Sereel's support for Canton means that institutions don't have to choose between the benefits of blockchain technology and the privacy standards their businesses require. They can leverage tokenization to improve efficiency, liquidity, and asset management while operating on infrastructure designed with enterprise and regulatory needs in mind.

By offering a privacy-focused network option on Canton, Sereel gives clients the flexibility to build where it makes the most sense for their institution. Whether the goal is broad market participation through established public ecosystems or confidential asset issuance and management through Canton.

For institutions exploring tokenization, the question is no longer whether blockchain can meet enterprise requirements. It's about choosing the right rails for the right assets, and Sereel is built to help make that choice possible.

By operating our own validator, Sereel sits on the exact same institutional rails as Goldman Sachs, the DTCC, and Euroclear, bringing the power of global financial utility to clients who want privacy, bridging the gap between cutting-edge tokenization technology and institutional-grade trust.

## Conclusion

The future of tokenization will not be defined by a single blockchain or network. Different assets, industries, and institutions have different requirements, and the infrastructure supporting them must be flexible enough to meet those needs. 

While public blockchains continue to drive innovation, liquidity, and open participation, privacy-focused networks like Canton are unlocking new possibilities for regulated financial markets and institutions that require greater confidentiality and control.

As the tokenization of real-world assets accelerates, the conversation is shifting from whether institutions should adopt blockchain technology to how they can choose the right infrastructure for their specific use cases. The ability to balance transparency, privacy, interoperability, and compliance will be a key factor in the next generation of digital asset markets.

At Sereel, we are building for that future by supporting a diverse ecosystem of blockchain networks. This multi-network approach gives institutions the flexibility to tokenize assets on the rails that best fit their operational, regulatory, and privacy requirements.

For organizations exploring tokenization, privacy is no longer a barrier to adoption. Whether the goal is broad market accessibility or institution-grade confidentiality, Sereel provides the infrastructure to help bring real-world assets on-chain with confidence, security, and the flexibility to build for the future of global finance.
